study.question: Can an explicit no_grad shortcut remove backward-only rank sorting from aligned-half inference while preserving the inherited forward function and all gradient-enabled behavior? Observed limitation: history_r0030_aligned_half.py _normalize_product computes detached donor ranking, gather, coefficient and cancelling surrogate even when gradients are disabled. The paired full/half receipts have inference_seconds17.70697/18.10318, p50 20.89873/21.36016ms and p95 21.85300/22.15223ms including feature gathering; timing alone does not establish the cause. Source inspection establishes avoidable operations, not their measured share of latency. Independent research seeds and checkpoint reuse are not exposed. This is a bounded implementation/cost study, not another adaptive score or gradient-mechanism sweep.
study.hypothesis: For a product p with finite representable norm, unit vector, donor scales and surrogate coefficient, u=p/sqrt(max(sum(p*p),1e-6)); the inherited half rule returns stopgrad(u)+(s-stopgrad(s)), where s=u times a detached finite coefficient. Under no_grad both copies of s have identical values, so directly returning u avoids detached donor sorting and surrogate construction. With gradients enabled the shortcut condition is false even in eval mode, preserving the inherited derivative and training arithmetic. Hypothesis: same-state outputs remain numerically equal and end-to-end inference cost falls. No claim that the existing half-gradient performance effect is explained or independently reproduced by this optimization. The equivalence domain excludes overflow/nonfinite intermediates in the old path; finite raw coordinates alone do not guarantee finite squared norms. Host natural-data finite-logit checks and synthetic probes are required; no universal floating-point equivalence is asserted.
